name: Hair tape-in / clip-in extensions

lead: Tape-in and clip-in extensions are wefts of human or synthetic hair attached to your own hair to add length and thickness immediately. People with thin or short hair use them to look fuller without a procedure or waiting for growth.

The wefts attach to natural hair, not the scalp, by clips or adhesive strips, adding visible density. They do not change the underlying hair or follicles, and clinical trials of their looks effect were not found.

paras: Clip-ins are fastened and removed by the wearer, often daily. Tape-ins are bonded to natural hair with adhesive strips, typically by a stylist, and stay in for a stretch before being re-taped or removed. They are one of several attachment methods that also include rings, fusion, weaving and wigs.

Dermatology references describe traction alopecia, hair loss at the hairline or around the ears, from prolonged tension. Adhesives can cause dermatitis or headaches, and patch testing before using bonding products is advised.

angle.text: Wefts attached to your natural hair by tape or clips add length and volume the moment they are fitted, with no waiting for growth. Clip-ins come out daily; the main documented risk is tension on natural hair.

lead: Tape-in and clip-in hair extensions are add-on wefts or strands of human or synthetic hair that attach to natural hair, using adhesive tape or small clips, to add length, volume or thickness. People use them to get a fuller head of hair or a longer style right away, including to disguise thinning at the crown or hairline [1].

Wikipedia lists tape-in and clip-in or clip-on among the main attachment methods for hair extensions, alongside micro or nano rings, fusion, weaving and wigs [1]. Clip-ins are put in and taken out by the wearer, whereas tape-ins are bonded to the hair for a period of weeks [1]. Human hair is the more durable option, while synthetic fibres such as Kanekalon are cheaper but less durable and can look stiffer [1].

Because the hair is attached to existing hair rather than the scalp, the effect is immediate and reversible, which is the main contrast with transplants or medication that work on the follicle. The best-documented concern is tension: traction alopecia, hair loss from ongoing pulling, is described by dermatology references as a result of tight styles and of extensions or weaves attached to tightly braided hair [2][3].
infobox: Human hair or synthetic fibre such as Kanekalon or Futura [1]
Clip-ins are removable by the wearer; a sew-in installation is reported to last about eight weeks [1]
Wigs, toupees, toppers, sew-ins, fusion, micro rings [1][4][5]

paras: Extensions come as wefts, which are strips of hair, or as single strands. Human hair is the premium material and most commonly comes from India, China and Vietnam; tangle-free versions have the cuticle chemically removed and a coating added for shine [1]. Synthetic fibres are cheaper and less durable, can be damaged by heat and friction, and heat styling tools generally are not used on them, although heat-resistant fibres exist [1].

Methods of integration listed on Wikipedia include track-and-sew, bonding glue, invisible-part techniques, thread sewing, tape-in and clip-in or clip-on [1]. Track-and-sew attaches wefts to cornrows; glue bonding is described as less popular because of health concerns; the invisible-part technique is designed to look like natural growth; and thread attachment avoids damage from bonding [1]. A sew-in invisible-part installation is reported to take about an hour and last roughly eight weeks [1].

Clip-ins are wefts fitted with small clips that the wearer snaps onto sections of their own hair. Wikipedia describes clips and adhesives as suited to adding bulk, and they are the version used for occasions where the wearer wants to add hair for a day and remove it the same evening [1].
Tape-ins are wefts bonded to the natural hair with adhesive tape. They stay in place for weeks rather than hours, which is why adhesive-related reactions are discussed alongside them [1].

Extensions descend from the long history of wigs and hairpieces. Wikipedia's wig article says ancient Egyptians shaved or cropped their hair and wore wigs, and that Assyrians, Phoenicians, Greeks and Romans also wore them as everyday fashion [4]. Wigs returned to Europe in the 1500s, helped by royal fashion: Louis XIII began wearing one in 1624, Charles II brought periwigs to England in 1660, and Louis XIV spread the trend in the 1660s [4]. Women of the eighteenth century typically wore hairpieces to supplement their own hair rather than full wigs [4].

Wigs were a fashion trend by the late seventeenth century [1]. Affordable synthetic modacrylic wigs arrived in the 1960s, making full wigs common for women [4]. Hair weaves appeared in the 1950s, initially among celebrities, and became widespread in the 1970s [1]. Toupees, which also attach to remaining natural hair, grew in popularity in the United States during the nineteenth century, with sales rising through the 1950s and 1960s [5].

Extensions are used to change hair length or add density without waiting for growth, and in grooming discussions they appear as a non-surgical way to add apparent hair volume. Wikipedia says wigs and extensions are worn by Black women, Orthodox Jewish women and people with medical conditions or treatment side effects, as well as for style [1].

For people with thinning hair the appeal is concealment. Pattern hair loss affects about half of men and a quarter of women by age 50, and hairpieces such as wigs or toupees are among the concealment options listed for larger areas [6]. Wikipedia notes that hair is closely tied to identity, for women often to femininity and attractiveness and for men to youth and vitality [6]. Attaching wefts at the thin crown or hairline is one approach people describe for blending added hair with remaining hair [1].

Most human hair used in weaves comes from Vietnam, India and China, and Wikipedia describes a large global trade in which India is a major exporter and hair from Hindu temples is prized [1]. Israeli rabbis banned temple-sourced hair for Jewish women's wigs in 2004 and again in 2017 [1]. Reports of exploitation in the hair trade, particularly involving women in the ASEAN region and India, have raised concerns, and the wig industry is described as multibillion-dollar [4].

Wikipedia reports that prolonged wear or tight attachment can cause traction alopecia, which may become permanent, and can cause breakage, split ends and damage to the follicles [1][2]. Glue-based methods have been linked to headaches, bald spots and dermatitis, and bonding wefts directly to the scalp can irritate it [1]. The toupee article says weaves attached to remaining hair can cause discomfort and traction alopecia over time [5].

Traction alopecia is mechanical rather than androgenic in cause. Typical triggers include tight ponytails, braids, weaves, extensions and dreadlocks, and chemical relaxers weaken the hair shaft and make breakage more likely [2]. Hair typically thins at the hairline, especially around the temples and sides, and a band of retained hair along the front edge, called the fringe sign, is a recognised clue [2][3]. DermNet describes early disease as non-scarring and possibly reversible if tension stops, with continued tension destroying follicles and leaving permanent scarring hair loss; itching, redness, scaling and many short broken hairs may appear [3].

Management centres on removing the tension. Options reported include loosening styles, avoiding chemicals and heat, and, for severe scarring cases, hair restoration surgery [2][3]. The condition is reported as one of the more common causes of hair loss in African American women, and also affects ballerinas and people who wear tight headgear for work or religion [2].

Hair systems and toupees, concealer fibres, wigs, and medical and surgical options for hair loss sit alongside extensions in the appearance-focused hair space [5][6]. The toupee article lists combing hair over a bald area, non-surgical hair systems, minoxidil, hair transplants and shaving the head as alternatives [5].

No studies found on tape-in or clip-in extensions for appearance. Dermatology descriptions of traction alopecia name tight styles, weaves and extensions attached to tightly braided hair as causes, with hairline recession at the temples and sides as the typical pattern [2][3].
